findings.source: study finding first-1 (details.html, "What the testers hit"; journal wf_13c0f539)
findings.title: Play on an answer keeps a board the reader picked earlier, so the asked-for table is not shown
where: skills/talk/static/call.js:1165 readerPlays() leaves follow as it is
skills/talk/static/call.js:1169 followAgain() only runs for a play of the board in front
skills/talk/static/call.js:863 only an automatic new answer turns following back on
findings.evidence: The persona clicked the Key points chip (follow turned off, Follow the voice button appeared), then pressed Play on answer 3, whose own board is the Boosters table. The voice read the table sentences but the stage stayed on Key points, with the caption 'The first dose teaches the lesson'. She lost the table she had asked for and had to work out the Follow the voice button.
findings.cause: By design (repo CLAUDE.md): a play the reader starts never turns following on, and a hand-picked board stays in front. But Play on a different answer's own message is a different intent from Play on the board in front. There is no sign on the panel that the voice is on a board that is not shown. Only a button on the stage says it.
findings.reproduced: code reading plus shots 17 and 18 (follow off after the chip click, Play pressed on answer 3)

skeptics.correction: Cite the Play button at call.js:334 as the entry point, not 863. Line 863 is only the board=true branch of playFrom, and the effective follow:false flag for the stage is at call.js:1190. Severity is probably medium rather than major. The Follow the voice button is visible in the stage header in shot 18, so the way out exists. The real gap is that nothing on the panel says the voice is on a board that is not shown. Shot 18 also shows the Key points chip highlighted while Boosters is the answer playing.

Three corrections. (1) Severity is overstated, because the page recovers with one click on Follow the voice, which is visible in the shot, and the persona's notes call it "Fine". Minor to moderate is fairer. (2) Key points is itself a board of answer 3 ("Key points: +1" chip), so the stage was not showing an unrelated board; it was showing the answer's other board instead of the Boosters table. (3) The line citations are imprecise: the Play button is call.js:334 and the answer-start follow logic is the audio "play" handler (~line 1190, follow: current.id !== readerAnswer), not line 863. This is by design in CLAUDE.md, so the real issue is a missing panel-side sign, or a policy choice for Play on a different answer's message.

Severity "major" is overstated. The page offers a clear, prominent recovery (the blue "Follow the voice" button on the stage), and the behaviour is documented and deliberate. Rate it minor to moderate. The line numbers are slightly off: the Play button on a message is call.js:334, and readerPlays and followAgain are at 1165 and 1169. The real gap is narrower than the finding states. Nothing on the side panel says the voice is on a board that is not in front, and Play on a different answer's own message is treated the same as Play on the board in front. The "Key points: +1" chip in answer 3's message also shows that answer 3 touched Key points. That makes it less clear that the table was the only board the voice should have shown.

findings.guard_proof: removed: 1 failed; restored: 1 passed; second test likewise
findings.notice: With a board you chose pinned, Play says which answer it starts and why, and the card has its own Play for the answer it shows.
findings.note: Play on another answer's row calls followAgain(), so its own board comes to the stage; the card's own Play keeps a pin, and the strip shows Pinned or Following.
findings.reopen_note: Round 2 (r2-tinkerer-5 carries study_match S-first-1; the sent-back rule applies). The fix made Play follow the board the reader pinned, as designed (S-first-1, S-listener-1), but the control now sits inside the answer-6 card and its label says 'Play answer 5', with 'Play starts answer 5.' in the Following strip; the card's own answer 6 cannot be played from that control until the reader presses Back to the voice. The label and note appear only while the audio is paused and only when the stage is pinned by hand. The page is not silent (the button and the strip both name answer 5) but the card never says why its number differs from the one it sits in. FIX: show both targets or label the board's answer explicitly ('Play answer 5 (the board you chose)', Greek too) and keep the card's own answer playable from the card; the aria-label and tooltip use the same text. Do not rename one control for another answer inside a card without saying why. GUARD: a test on the pinned-and-paused state that the transport names its target with the reason and that answer 6 stays playable.

findings.source: study finding first-2 (details.html, "What the testers hit"; journal wf_13c0f539)
findings.title: Hover tooltip of the Send button covers the player time readout and stays up
where: skills/talk/static/call.css:214 .ib[data-tip]:hover::after is placed bottom:calc(100% + 8px) on the composer buttons
skills/talk/static/call.html:50 #sendtext data-tip=Send, disabled but still hoverable
findings.evidence: A 'Send' tooltip sits above the Send button at the bottom right and hides the left half of the '0:15 / 0:15' timer. It shows in every screenshot after the first message, even when Send is disabled, so the persona read it as a stuck label.
findings.cause: The tooltip is hover-only, and the pointer stays on Send after a click, so it stays up. Composer buttons put it above the button, where the timer sits, and a disabled button still shows it. The persona's pointer position is likely what kept it up.
findings.reproduced: code reading; the shots show the pointer parked on Send after each click

skeptics.correction: The tooltip is a normal hover tooltip and is not stuck. It shows only while the pointer rests on Send, and it goes away when the pointer moves. A real mouse user who clicks Send and leaves the pointer there would see the same thing, so this is not only a harness artifact. It also does not hide "the left half" of the timer. In the shot it covers the lower part of the left half of the readout ("0:15", which is partly cut off). Severity stays minor. The suggested fix is to suppress the tooltip on disabled buttons with :not(:disabled), or to place the composer tooltips so they do not cover the time readout.

Keep the finding as minor. The cause is the pointer resting on the disabled Send button after a click, not a stuck label. The relevant CSS is call.css lines 211 to 214, in the `@media (hover:hover)` block. The tooltip overlaps the player time only while the pointer is on the composer buttons. A fix would suppress the tooltip on disabled buttons, or place it elsewhere. The call.html line is the `#sendtext` button, around line 50.

Four corrections. (1) Line numbers: the tooltip rule is around call.css lines 212-216 and the Send button is call.html line 50, which matches. (2) Overstated persistence: the tooltip is hover-only and the pointer is parked on Send by Playwright after each click. A real user who clicks Send keeps the pointer there only until they move it, and one who presses Enter never triggers it. Describe it as "a tooltip covers the timer while the pointer rests on Send", not "stays up". (3) Overlap: the tooltip hides the right half of the timer in the shot, not the left half. (4) The "every screenshot" claim is a harness effect of the parked pointer. A narrower fix is to suppress the tooltip on a disabled Send, or to place the composer tooltips elsewhere.

findings.guard: none: tooltip placement is CSS, proved by shots
findings.guard_proof: none
findings.notice: Resting the pointer on Send no longer hides the player time.
findings.note: Fixed by the tooltip rework (QF-2): a disabled Send has no tip and a hover tip opens left of the composer buttons after a delay and fades.

findings.source: study finding first-3 (details.html, "What the testers hit"; journal wf_13c0f539)
findings.title: Waiting state is a bare 'Claude is working…' with no time or progress and a blank conversation
where: skills/talk/static/call.js:527 view.working with no running activity gives the fixed text 'Claude is working…'; the elapsed seconds appear only when an activity item is running
skills/talk/talk.py:2812 activity is sent only while turns.working
findings.evidence: For 2 to 3.5 minutes after Send the panel showed only 'Claude is working…' with a pulsing edge. The stage said 'The stage is empty' and nothing gave an elapsed time or an estimate, so she wondered if it was stuck.
findings.cause: The elapsed time is shown only when the session's activity hook reports a running tool. The harness responder had no hook, so the text stayed fixed. In a real session the label would be 'tool · Ns'. The panel has no elapsed counter of its own as a fallback. The slowness itself is out of scope.
findings.reproduced: code reading; shot 03

skeptics.correction: Two corrections. First, the conversation is not blank: shot 03 shows the user's own typed message as a bubble, and only the answer area is empty. Second, the page does have a fallback for a stuck turn. After STALLED_OPEN_AFTER, view.stalled shows "Claude has not picked this up yet. Check the terminal...". That check comes before the working text at call.js:524-525, so the persona may simply not have waited long enough to see it. The line numbers are slightly off: the code is at call.js:525-528, and the view() payload is at talk.py:~2811, not 2812. The claim that real sessions would show "tool · Ns" depends on the activity hook reporting, which I did not verify.

Say the 2 to 3.5 minute bare label is mostly a harness artifact, because the responder had no activity hook. In a real session the label becomes "tool · Ns" while a tool runs. The gap remains for stretches with no running tool, where the panel shows a fixed "Claude is working…" with no timer of its own. Rate it minor. The cause and line references are right.

Two corrections. (1) Shot 11 shows the page does list activity lines in the conversation ("thinking of a story for kids", "finding a simpler way"), so the responder did report activity. The cause is therefore not "no hook at all" but that no item was in state "running", so the counter was not used. (2) The cited talk.py:2812 is the view() line that sends activity only while turns.working. The label and seconds come from activity_view() at about line 2376. A turn with no running activity falls back to the fixed text, in real sessions as well as in the harness.

findings.title: Voice speed is only in the gear and its voice description is jargon
where: skills/talk/static/call.html:85 settings popover holds Voice speed
skills/talk/static/call.html:41 player row has back, play and scrubber but no speed control
findings.evidence: She asked Claude to slow down and it only rephrased. The speed control was found only after hunting in Settings. The Voice line reads 'VoiceStudio on this Mac, profile silent: free, slower', which means nothing to her.
findings.cause: Speed lives only in the gear popover. The Voice description is the engine name and profile text straight from the server, written for the owner of the machine. The engine text itself is partly a harness stand-in.
findings.reproduced: shot 12 and code reading

skeptics.correction: Two corrections. First, the cited lines are off: the speed control is at call.html:90 (not 85), and the engine text is built in call.js:13-18. Second, the jargon part is overstated. "profile silent" is a harness artifact. A real VoiceStudio user sees a real profile name. An Azure user sees "Azure: fast, billed per character", which is plainer. "Speed is only in the gear" is real, but the severity is minor.

The profile name "silent" comes from the harness stand-in. A real session would show something like "profile Talk". The line would still be jargon, but this exact text is not what a user meets. The code line numbers are roughly right: the speed control is at call.html:90, not 85, and the jargon string is built in call.js:15-17. Keep the severity minor. The cause is the placement of the speed control in the gear popover and the engine-oriented Voice text.

1) The Voice text is not 'straight from the server'. It is a literal template in skills/talk/static/call.js:14-19, and only the profile name comes from CFG.voice. The word 'silent' is a harness stand-in profile name, so a real user would see their own profile name. The jargon ('VoiceStudio', 'profile', 'free, slower') is still real. 2) The Voice line is at call.html:84, not 85. Line 85 is the 'I speak' block and the Voice speed block is at line 86 or 87. 3) The Voice jargon and the speed-control discoverability are two separate minor issues merged into one. The jargon does not hinder finding the speed control. 4) Severity should be low or minor at most. Voice speed is clearly labelled in Settings with 0.75x to 1.5x buttons. A 'check' stop offers 'Again, slower' (call.js:1118-1122), but only when the answer carries a stop. The persona's real friction, that asking Claude to slow down only got a rephrase, is a content and responder issue and not the page's. Only the speed control's discoverability belongs to the page.

findings.source: study finding first-6 (details.html, "What the testers hit"; journal wf_13c0f539)
findings.title: Table board drew its three columns into two header columns and cell text overlapped
where: skills/stage/static/stage.js:550-600 shapeBoard builds the colgroup and wordFloors
skills/stage/static/stage.css:550 .md.grid col width:max(var(--w),var(--min))
skills/talk/talk.py:857 check_table pads and cuts rows to the header width
findings.evidence: The Boosters table showed the headers 'SHOT' and 'MEMORY' run together and 'BOOSTER' in the second slot. In the rows 'First dose' overlapped 'new' and 'Months later' overlapped 'fading'. The table could not be used on a board.
findings.cause: Not settled. The responder said the table had 3 columns, but the header drew as two columns, so either the header count and the cell count differ in the stored source or the fixed table layout puts three cells into two column tracks. I could not reproduce it.
findings.reproduced: not reproduced; shots only

skeptics.correction: The cause is not a header/cell count mismatch. The table does have three columns. The first column is drawn only about 40 px wide, which is less than its own padding plus its words. The second column then starts almost at the first, and the third gets about 200 px. Cell text overflows the first column into the second's slot, which looks like "two header columns". So the fault is in the column widths of the fixed-layout table (stage.css .md.grid col{width:max(var(--w),var(--min))}, the colgroup widths and the wordFloors --min floors in stage.js, roughly lines 570-640), not in talk.py check_table. The cited line numbers are about right. I did not isolate the exact variable. Severity major is fair, since the table is unreadable on the board. It is stage-only. The finding's "not reproduced" is wrong: it reproduces with a plain 3x3 table of short words at 1440 px.

Keep the finding as a real stage rendering bug with an unknown cause, and mark the cause as unconfirmed. The check_table pad-and-cut path in talk.py is probably not the cause, since the header text does show three headers. The shapeBoard colgroup is built from max(heads, row cells), so it should be 3 columns; the likelier suspects are CSS layout of the first (`key`, sticky) column or the colgroup/--min widths, which needs a browser reproduction with the stored table source. Severity "major" is fair because the table cannot be read.

The analyst's own hypothesis ("header count and cell count differ in the stored source") does not fit the shots. The header shows three labels, SHOT, MEMORY and BOOSTER, and each row shows three cells, so the data is consistent. The defect is column widths: columns 1 and 2 are far too narrow for their text and column 3 is too wide. The likely cause is the colgroup widths, or a `--min` or `--w` value computed from `wordFloors` or `widths`, not the header count. Suspect `.md.grid col{width:max(var(--w),var(--min))}` (stage.css:550) under a fixed table layout. Check whether `wordFloors` ran before the fonts loaded or while the wrap had `clientWidth` 0, and whether the table's `--tw` width was narrower than the sum of the floors. The cited `check_table` in talk.py is probably not involved, because the row and header counts match. Keep the severity as major for the stage, since the table is unreadable. Mark the cause as unconfirmed until reproduced with a three-column table of short words such as Shot, Memory and Booster.

findings.guard_proof: see QF-7: fails with the fix removed (1 failed in 0.15s), passes restored (1 passed in 0.12s)
findings.notice: The Boosters table shows three columns, Shot, Booster and Memory, each readable, with nothing overlapping.
findings.note: Same root cause as QF-7 (the first column drawn 40 px wide because a % and px max() on a col is read as auto); not a header/cell count mismatch. Reproduced with the exact Boosters table; fixed by px column widths with floors held.

findings.source: study finding phone-1 (details.html, "What the testers hit"; journal wf_13c0f539)
findings.title: Stalled warning tells a phone user to 'check the terminal' and offers no way out
where: skills/talk/static/call.js:524 fixed stalled text, shown for every viewer
skills/talk/live_turns.py:15,166-169 STALLED_OPEN_AFTER=180s sets view.stalled
findings.evidence: The first question waited about 4.5 minutes. After 3 minutes the foot showed an orange 'Claude has not picked this up yet. Check the terminal: the session may be waiting for a permission.' The persona has no terminal and could not tell whether to wait, resend or cancel. The slowness came from the responder (it stalled on a stray stdin command), which is a harness cause, but the wording and the missing action belong to the panel.
findings.cause: The stalled line is a single developer-facing string. It assumes the viewer sits at the Claude Code terminal. It has no action (resend, cancel, copy the question) and no plain-language alternative for someone who only has the call page.
findings.reproduced: code reading plus the screenshot at 190 s; the delay itself is a harness artifact (responder log: lost about four minutes to its own error)

skeptics.correction: Correct the cited stall timing in live_turns.py. Lines 15 and 166-169 give two thresholds, not one. STALLED_AFTER is 20 s (line 12) and applies when nothing is open and the turn is still pending. STALLED_OPEN_AFTER is 180 s and applies when the session is working on an older turn or has collected a turn and not answered it. The persona's 3-minute warning matches the 180 s case, where a turn was collected but never answered. The stalled() code is lines 160-172. Also, the page does have a "working" state with shimmer and activity labels before the stall. Severity "major" may be a little high: the warning is accurate for a developer, and the phone-user gap is the wording and the missing action.

Lower the severity from major to moderate or minor. Say that "check the terminal" fits the usual user who started /talk from a terminal, and that the gap is for someone on a phone or another machine, and in having no action. The 4.5-minute wait was a harness artifact, so the finding rests on the wording and the missing action, not on the delay. Line references are correct: call.js:524 and live_turns.py:15,166-169.

Reduce severity from major to minor or moderate. The wording and the missing action are real, but the page stays usable and the "check the terminal" hint is valid for the usual viewer who started the call. Line 524 is the main cause; the live_turns.py lines cited are only the trigger. Another cause of the stall is possible: the first branch of stalled() fires at 180 s for a collected turn that was never answered. The suggested fix is a wording that also works with no terminal, for example "Claude is taking long. You can wait or send it again", plus a Send again or copy-question action beside it. The persona's claim that she "could not tell whether to wait, resend or cancel" is partly a reading of the screenshot, since the page never says what the state means.

findings.title: On a phone with a board up, the conversation is about three lines tall and clips the newest question
where: skills/talk/static/call.css:280-282 --ph 46% and 38% when [data-board], not adjustable
skills/talk/static/call.js:386-414 render() pins the conversation to its end (scrollTop = scrollHeight), so the tall newest group pushes the question above the visible top
skills/talk/static/call.js:524-532 status line takes a further row in the foot
findings.evidence: With a board shown the panel is 38% of the screen. The header, the player and the text field take most of that, so the conversation window is roughly 150 css px. The reader sees a one-line folded answer cut with an ellipsis and has to tap Show text and scroll a tiny window. The user's own typed question is cut off under the header, with only its last line ('anything', 'to 1 to 1 versus 1 to 2 to 2') visible.
findings.cause: The phone layout gives the stage a fixed share and the stage wins when a board is up. The conversation shows its end, and when the end (status line, chip row, answer card) is taller than the box, the user's own message that started the exchange scrolls out of view. There is no drag handle and no way to hide the stage.
findings.reproduced: code reading and three screenshots (15, 24, 27) showing the same clipped question; not re-run

skeptics.correction: Severity "major" looks overstated. The conversation is an ordinary scrolling chat, and the clipped question is above the newest answer, so the user can scroll up to it. The one-line answer is by design (the repo CLAUDE.md says every answer folds to one line in the panel). The cause is partly wrong: the question scrolls out of view mainly because the box is short, not because of the status line (call.js:524-532, which I did not verify). The point that holds is that 38% is fixed and the stage cannot be hidden or resized. I would call it moderate or minor.

The severity is overstated. The conversation is a normal scrollable chat pinned to its newest end, so the older question is scrolled off, not lost, and one swipe brings it back. The answer folds to one line by design, and Show text opens it. Calling the question "clipped" is a reading of ordinary scroll position. It is a cramped panel (about 160 px) on phones while a board is up, which is minor to moderate. I also did not check the cited call.js lines (386-414 and 524-532), so treat the pinning cause and the extra status row in the foot as plausible, not confirmed.

Severity is overstated: major should be minor to moderate. The answer stays readable through Show text and scrolling, and the clipped user question is context, not lost content. In shot 27 the stage is a resting bar chart with large empty space below it, so the fixed 38% share is wasteful there. The claim of "no way to hide the stage" is only partly true. The fullscreen button in the header and the rail toggle exist, though neither is an obvious way to give the panel more height. Line 524-532 (status line) is a minor contributor, not the main cause. The main causes are the fixed --ph share at call.css 280-282 and the pin-to-end scroll.

findings.guard_proof: none

findings.title: Follow the voice button squeezes the stage header to 'F...'
where: skills/stage/static/stage.css:50-54 .follow button, margin and padding fixed
skills/stage/static/stage.js:109,1346 follow button placed beside the history buttons
skills/stage/static/stage.js:1174 pane headers start after the history buttons and the button
findings.evidence: After tapping an older board chip, the blue 'Follow the voice' button appears in the stage header at 390 px and pushes the board title down to a truncated 'F...' with only the icon. The persona did not know what the button meant.
findings.cause: The button has a fixed text label and 12 px padding and shares one row with the history arrows, the board counter and the title. No narrow-width variant (icon only, or its own row) exists, so the title is the part that gives way.
findings.reproduced: screenshot 24; code reading

skeptics.correction: The line references are slightly off. The `.follow` rule is at stage.css 49-54 (the comment at 49 and the rule at 50-54). The button markup is at stage.js:109 and the show/hide logic at ~1349-1355, not 1346. The title is squeezed by the `--navw` reservation at stage.js ~1175-1178. The "F..." is the board's title, not the button. The button itself reads "Follow the voice" in full in the shot. Severity "minor" fits: the board is still readable, and only the title is cut.

findings.title: Table board: RATIO header overlaps STARTER and ratio cells break one word per line
where: skills/stage/static/stage.js wordFloors and --min on col (CLAUDE.md: a table column is never narrower than its longest word)
skills/stage/static/stage.css table column sizing
findings.evidence: On a 390 px phone the Feeding ratios table draws the header 'RATIO' over 'STARTER' (letters overlap) and the first column's '1 to 1 to 1' wraps to one word per line, making each row tall. This is the board's layout, not the chat panel.

skeptics.correction: Keep it, but the cause is unproven, so treat the persona's account as a guess. Candidates from the code: (1) `wordFloors` returns early when `wrap.clientWidth` is 0 or the canvas context is missing. (2) The words are measured before the web font loads, so the fallback font gives a narrower floor. (3) A 390 px board where `padSum + wordSum` exceeds the width and `tf` is below 1. The measured floor does not cover the `th` text, which has letter-spacing .06em at 10.5px times `--tf`. Also, `wordFloors` only sets `--min` on cols, and the fixed table layout may ignore it. The cited code lines are roughly right (stage.js 607-640, stage.css 586-590). Severity "major" is fair for a phone table, but it is stage-only.

The cause is not traced, only guessed. I did not re-run it either. The most likely lead is that wordFloors measured the words before the web font had loaded, or measured with a different font or letter-spacing than the one drawn. That would also explain why the floor is wrong for "RATIO" in particular. Part of the one-word-per-line wrapping is by design: the floor is the longest word, so a phrase like "1 to 1 to 1" can wrap between words in a narrow column. The real defect is the overlap, meaning the column ended up narrower than its longest word. "Major" is fair for a phone user, but the table is still readable apart from the header collision.

Split the finding into two parts. (1) The header overlap is the real bug. wordFloors in skills/stage/static/stage.js (about lines 607-637) sets --min for the RATIO column too small, or the header text overflows its cell. Likely causes are a canvas measure done before the webfont loaded, or letter-spacing and uppercase not matching what is drawn. (2) The one-word-per-line wrap is not a violation of the floor rule. The rule only guarantees that the longest single word ("1" or "to") does not break, so a multi-word cell wraps at every space in a 40 px column. The real problem is that the fit-mode column widths (--wp) give the ratio column almost nothing, so it is better described as a column-share problem than as a broken word floor. The wrap exists in the shot too, but it is a side effect of the narrow column. Severity "major" looks a little high for a stage-only layout glitch; "moderate" fits better. The table is readable but ugly, and the overlap makes the header text hard to read.

findings.title: Stage board overflow and table overlap on the TV stage
where: skills/stage/static/stage.js wordFloors (table columns) and zoom handling by stage:zoom
skills/talk/static/call.js:119 toStage stage:zoom TV_ZOOM 1.35
findings.evidence: In TV mode the bars board for Pressure by depth runs past the bottom: the 5 bar chip and the last bar sit on the edge and the board is cut. Side notes on the sequence board are small grey monospace and the diagram uses only the top third of the stage.
findings.cause: The stage draws these boards at the TV zoom. The zoom is not fitted to the pane (bars) and the table's column floors do not account for it. This is the stage and not the panel.
findings.reproduced: seen in shots 08, 17 and 19; not re-run

skeptics.correction: Three corrections. (1) Shot 08 shows the sequence board at the normal desk size, with the panel at a different width and the expand icon in the header, not the TV layout of 17 and 19. The "diagram uses only the top third" point is therefore a general sequence-board issue and not TV-specific. (2) The cause is not verified. The code gives no sign that wordFloors accounts for the zoom, but it could instead be a mismatch between the "--tw" ch width and the larger TV font. The bars overflow is not tied to a missing fit-to-pane in the code I read. (3) The finding is stage-only and, as the persona rated it, major for the table overlap (unreadable words) and minor for the sequence-board sizing.

The cause is a hypothesis, not confirmed. The layout code (`wordFloors`, `fitScale`) measures widths and fits the pane while the root element is CSS-zoomed. Under CSS zoom those measurements may not match what is drawn, so the column floors and the pane fit are off. Check this before assigning blame to `wordFloors` alone. The `call.js` line number is 119 for the `toStage` call, and the `TV_ZOOM` constant is at line 298. The table also floats small in the middle of the stage (shot 19), which is a separate layout point from the overlap. The sequence-board remarks are unverified and should be dropped or checked separately.

Treat the cause as a hypothesis: the zoom-related mismatch is plausible but unproven. `wordFloors` (stage.js:607) measures words with a canvas at computed font sizes and compares them to `wrap.clientWidth`. Under CSS zoom those two may be in different units, which would explain a column floor that is too small. The `fitScale` logic for the bars board also may not account for the zoom. Neither was tested. The call.js line is 119 in the first `toStage` call, with the same call repeated at call.js:1733. The sequence-board remark (small grey monospace notes, diagram only in the top third) was not checked against the cited shots. I read only 17 and 19, not 08. The cut-off bars board may be reachable by scrolling the pane, so "cut" may be overstated, but the clipped chip on first view is real. Severity "major" is fair for TV mode only. It is stage-only, as the finding says.

RESTORED: '1 passed in 0.13s' and '2 passed in 0.13s'. Browser: .stage bottom 1458 before, 1080 after.

A table narrower than 34rem now draws at least that wide. skeptics.correction: Two details are slightly off. First, the line numbers are 212-216 for showPop and 218 for the Escape handler, not 212-219 and 221. Second, Escape does not return focus to the gear. Focus never left the gear when the popup opened, so it is simply still there. A user who clicks into the popup and then presses Escape would lose focus, because nothing moves it back to the gear. Severity "major" is arguable. Escape works, and a mouse user is unaffected. It is an accessibility gap for keyboard-only users.

The Escape claim is partly wrong. The Escape handler (about line 221) only calls showPop(null) and has no focus-return code. Focus stays on the gear only because it was never moved. If a user has already tabbed into the popup, Escape hides it and focus drops to the body rather than returning to the gear. Shot 22 may show the first case, where focus was never moved. Escape does not return focus to the gear, because focus never left it. The Escape handler (call.js line 221) only calls showPop(null). The same gap applies to pCalls, and to railgear, which opens the same pGear popup. "No focus trap" is not itself a defect for a non-modal popover. The real gap is that focus does not move into the popup on open, and that it does not return to the opener when the popup closes. Screen-reader users can jump by landmark. The gap is for keyboard-only sighted users, who have no shortcut. Line 1459-1463 is the type-anywhere handler, which does not apply when something is already focused. Moving the text box or player earlier in the Tab order would work as a fix. A minor or moderate accessibility gap (no skip link or shortcut to the text box, player or stage) is a fairer description. The cited line range 1459-1463 is correct. Say "no skip link or key to jump to the text box, player or stage". Drop "landmark-free", since the panel has labelled aside, section and toolbar regions. Cite the guard in the typing handler (call.js ~1459-1463), which does nothing once any element has focus, rather than only "focused on load or by typing". skeptics.correction: Minor: the toast's retry button is labelled "Retry" in call.html:68, not "Send again", unless call.js changes it. I did not find where "Send again" is set. The central claim stands: the status line and the conversation are not live regions. "Major" severity is reasonable for a screen reader user, since waiting and answer arrival are the call's core feedback.

Minor: the toast's retry button says "Retry" in call.html:68, not "Send again". "Send again" may be set dynamically in call.js, which I did not check. The call.js line refs are roughly right (paintInfo is near 460-464). Also note that a naive aria-live on #convo would re-read the per-word highlight spans, so the fix should target #status plus a short "Claude answered" announcement.

Two small corrections. First, the toast's retry button is labelled "Retry" in call.html (line 68), not "Send again". "Send again" is probably another toast string, or the persona misread it. The toast being the only live region is still true. Second, "major" is arguable. Status and answers are announced nowhere, which is a real accessibility gap for a screen-reader user waiting on slow answers. But the page is fully operable and the information can be read by navigating, so "moderate" may fit better. Cite call.js lines for the status and convo rendering from the current file, since the cited numbers were not checked.

findings.source: study finding screenreader-2 (details.html, "What the testers hit"; journal wf_13c0f539)
findings.title: A board opening on the stage, and stepping through it, is not announced
where: skills/talk/static/call.js:149-154 (chipTap and front cues move the stage by postMessage only)
skills/talk/static/call.js:349 (the chip's aria-label is the only text of the board in the panel)
skills/talk/static/call.html:15 (the stage is an iframe titled 'Stage')
findings.evidence: When an answer arrives the stage jumps to the table or chart. Nothing says so. Daniel learned of it only from the 'On the stage: Yearly fees' button in the conversation. Stepping with Next step did not announce which row was current.
findings.cause: Following the voice and fronting a board are visual postMessage calls to a cross-origin iframe. The panel emits no text for them and no focus or live update. The stage's own frame announcement is stage-only.
findings.reproduced: code reading only; the stage-side step announcement was not checked in the stage code.

skeptics.correction: Narrow the claim about stepping. The panel emits no step announcement, but the stage side was not checked by the persona. lanes.js:121 has an explicit aria-live="off" on .ln-now, so a lanes board suppresses announcements on purpose. screenboard.js:33 has a polite live region (.sb-text) that may announce steps for that board kind. For table boards, stage-side announcement is unverified, so "stepping did not announce the row" should not be stated as a panel fact. The chip does exist in the conversation as a reachable button, so a screen reader user can find it by browsing. What is missing is the live announcement. The shots could not show announcements, so the persona's observation came from the accessibility tree or from reading the code. Severity "major" is arguable, and "moderate" is more likely.

Narrow the claim. The panel lacks the announcement, but stage/static/lanes.js and screenboard.js do contain aria-live, so step announcement for those board types may exist inside the iframe. The persona did not check this, and I did not check whether a table board has it. Whether the announcement works for the Next step case is unverified, so the "major" severity for stepping is uncertain. The call.js line numbers cited were not verified.

The scope is wider than the finding says: the stage side has no announcement either. The stage has no live region or `aria-current` for the current table row or step. Only screenboard.js:33 (polite) and lanes.js:121 (`aria-live="off"`) mention live regions. Line 349 of call.js labels the chip, which is a button in the panel. It does not announce anything. "Major" may be a little high: the chip and the reader text do give a screen-reader user a way to find the board. The missing announcement of a board opening and of the current step is real.

findings.guard_proof: removed: 1 failed in 0.23s | restored: 1 passed in 0.22s

findings.note: A board that the stage fronts, and a chip pin, are announced through announce(); stepping inside a board is the stage's own and was not changed.

findings.source: study finding screenreader-3 (details.html, "What the testers hit"; journal wf_13c0f539)
findings.title: The 'Key points: +1' chip reads as cryptic and does nothing the reader can detect
where: skills/talk/talk.py:2660 (self.add('board', f'Key points: +{added}', view=KEY_VIEW, kind='points'))
skills/talk/static/call.js:349 (for kind points the aria-label is the bare text, with no 'On the stage')
skills/talk/static/call.js:150-154 (a press only fronts the board and turns Follow off)
findings.evidence: The chip is read aloud as 'Key points: +1'. Daniel did not know what +1 meant or what pressing it would do. After pressing it he detected no change, so it felt dead.
findings.cause: The chip label is a counter meant for sighted scanning. The aria-label for points drops the 'On the stage:' prefix that other chips get. Pressing it changes only the stage in a separate iframe, and the panel gives no feedback. It also silently turns off 'Stage follows the voice'.
findings.reproduced: code reading

skeptics.correction: Minor: the points chip is deliberately exempted from the "On the stage:" prefix (an explicit ternary), so it is a design choice that reads badly, not an oversight. The cause is also not only the label. The same press brings the Key points board to the front and turns Follow off, and the panel does repaint its settings and reader. The missing piece is an announcement or visible feedback for the stage change. Severity "major" is probably overstated for a chip that is only a convenience shortcut.

Narrow the "does nothing" claim. For a sighted user, pressing the chip does visibly front the Key points board on the stage. In shot 09 that board shows Answer 1 and Answer 2 as numbered cards, and the header reads "Key points". The dead feeling is specific to a screen-reader user, because the stage is a separate iframe and nothing in the panel announces the change. The missing "On the stage:" prefix for points chips is real but looks deliberate in the code, since the line was written to treat points chips differently. Severity "major" is a little high. This is a label and feedback gap, not a blocker. The silent Follow-off is accurate, and the code does it on purpose.

Severity "major" looks overstated. This is a minor labelling and feedback gap, because the chip does front the board on the stage. Two details need care. (1) The prefix drop looks deliberate, so "Key points: +1" reads as a label of its own. The fix is wording, such as "On the stage: Key points, 1 added", plus a polite live-region announcement when it is pressed. (2) Follow is turned off only when it was on, and paintSettings updates the gear switch, so "silently" is only partly true: it is silent to a screen reader and visible on screen. The cited line numbers are off. The aria-label line is about 349 in call.js, but the chipTap code sits near lines 146-154.

findings.guard_proof: removed: 1 failed in 0.23s | restored: 1 passed in 0.22s
findings.notice: Pressing a chip visibly pins the stage and says so.
findings.note: The chip label names Key points, carries Show on the stage in its aria-label, shows aria-pressed when its board is in front, and a press is announced and shown on the Following strip.

findings.source: study finding screenreader-4 (details.html, "What the testers hit"; journal wf_13c0f539)
findings.title: The conversation has no headings, per-answer landmarks or latest-answer jump
where: skills/talk/static/call.js:314-315 (turns are div.turn with a div.who 'You' or 'Claude', no heading or article)
skills/talk/static/call.js:327-328 (status entries kept as div.line.status)
skills/talk/static/call.html:32 (#convo has no log role)
findings.evidence: User text, status lines, chip rows and answers run together in the tree. There is nothing to jump to with H, and the newest answer must be found by scanning. A stale 'thinking it through' status line stays in the history between turns.
findings.cause: Entries are built from generic divs. 'Claude answer N' is split between a 'who' div and an 'answer N' label rather than one heading or labelled article. Status lines are stored as entries and never removed.
findings.reproduced: code reading; the stale status line is visible in the screenshot

skeptics.correction: Minor. #convo is a labelled section, which is a region landmark, so it is not entirely unmarked. Only the log role and live announcement are missing. The status line is a div.line.status. The status line is a real kept entry, but whether it reads as stale depends on the timing. Severity minor is fair.

The conversation container is not unlabelled. call.html:32 is a section with aria-label="Conversation", so it is a named region. It lacks role=log or aria-live. Say "no heading or article per turn and no latest-answer jump", not "no landmark". The line numbers are call.js ~314-320 and ~343 (the cited 327-328 is slightly off). The stale status line is real, since status entries are kept as entries.

Two corrections. (1) call.html:32 is not an unlabelled container. #convo is a <section aria-label="Conversation">, which is a region landmark. What is missing is role="log" or aria-live and per-answer structure, not a label. (2) Status lines are stored entries by design, and talk.py:2147 gives them the label "Claude, working". The stale-line complaint is that they are never cleared or collapsed once the answer arrives. Keep the severity at minor.

findings.guard_proof: WITHOUT (the focus call removed from jumpLatest): 1 failed in 0.23s | WITH: 1 passed in 0.23s
findings.notice: The first tab stop in the panel jumps straight to the newest answer.

The per-answer headings, the named list and the removal of stale status rows are in batch C's Now card and earlier list (h3 Earlier, listitem rows, no progress-note rows), which I read on the C branch but did not build. findings.source: study finding screenreader-5 (details.html, "What the testers hit"; journal wf_13c0f539)
findings.title: Autoplay talks over a screen reader, and the Play button keeps changing its name
where: skills/talk/static/call.js:284 (autoplay defaults to true)
skills/talk/static/call.js:823-847 (a new answer plays by itself)
skills/talk/static/call.js:423 (per-answer button text is 'Pause' or '▶ Play', with no aria-label)
skills/talk/static/call.js:557 (the foot button's aria-label cycles Pause, Play again and Play)
skills/talk/static/call.html:91 (the 'Play new answers by themselves' toggle exists in Settings)
findings.evidence: An answer starts playing aloud by itself over the screen reader. The play control reads 'Pause', then '▶ Play', then 'Play again', and one of those names contains a glyph.
findings.cause: Autoplay is on by default with nothing to detect a screen reader. The 'Play new answers by themselves' toggle exists but is inside the Settings popover. The per-answer buttons use visible text with a ▶ glyph as their name and have no aria-pressed.
findings.reproduced: code reading. Daniel missed the autoplay toggle because he did not see the popover contents.

skeptics.correction: Cite call.js:283 for the autoplay default, not 284. Say the foot play/pause button's changing label is normal toggle behaviour. The real defects are the "▶" glyph in the per-answer button's name, built from textContent, and the lack of aria-pressed or aria-label on it. Autoplay by default is a policy choice. A browser blocks audio before a user gesture, and the call is started by the user, so this is minor at most.

Narrow the claim. (1) The foot button's changing name (Pause / Play again / Play) is an ordinary play/pause toggle with a clean aria-label and is not a defect; drop it. (2) The real defect is small: the per-answer button (call.js:333, 423) uses visible text "▶ Play" as its name, so a screen reader may read the glyph, and it carries no aria-pressed or aria-label. It also differs from the foot button, which says "Play again". (3) Autoplay over a screen reader is by design with a settings switch, so it is a discoverability and design point. Its cause is not a bug, and the "reproduced" evidence is code reading plus a persona who missed the popover. Severity stays minor.

Keep it as minor, scoped to the panel. Narrow the claim. The real issues are (1) the per-answer button's accessible name starts with a "▶" glyph, "▶ Play", and has no aria-label, while the foot button has one, so the two controls name the same action differently ("Play" vs "▶ Play"); and (2) autoplay is on by default and its off switch is only in the Settings popover, so a screen reader user cannot find it quickly. The cycling Pause, Play again and Play on the foot button is a standard state label and is not a defect. Point 2 is better framed as 'autoplay has no quick off switch outside Settings' than as 'nothing detects a screen reader'.

findings.guard_proof: call-return.js reverted: both 1 failed; restored: both 1 passed
findings.notice: The Autoplay switch is found by saying Autoplay and tells a screen reader what it did when pressed.
findings.note: A quick Play new answers by themselves switch (aria-pressed, icon) sits at the end of the state strip and drives the gear's own switch. The glyph in the per-answer Play name is gone in batch C's list rows, which are labelled Play answer N (read on the C branch, not built here).
findings.reopen_note: Round 2 (r2-power-1 carries study_match S-screenreader-5; the sent-back rule applies). The strip's Autoplay switch has aria-label 'Play new answers by themselves' (strip.autoplay.aria) while its visible word is 'Autoplay', so name-based tools and voice control ('click Play', 'click Autoplay') pick the wrong control: Dev clicked the button named Play and flipped Autoplay off, the next answer never played by itself and the only sign was the strip changing. The toggle also gives no explicit announce(); aria-pressed is updated (call-return.js:179), so assistive tech reports the state on the focused control, and the visible text flips between 'Autoplay on' and 'Autoplay off'. FIX: make the accessible name start with the visible word, for example 'Autoplay: new answers play by themselves', keep aria-pressed for the state (do not also put the state in the name), keep the settings row #autoplay as is, update the Greek strip.autoplay.aria (call-i18n.js lines 255-259 area), and announce the change once through #announcer from the click handler (call-return.js:189) and a change listener on #autoplay added in call-return.js (call-input.js:150 stays untouched). The note truncation seen in the same shots is r2-first-2. GUARD: a test that the aria-label of #ssauto starts with the visible word in both languages and that a toggle announces once.

findings.source: study finding screenreader-6 (details.html, "What the testers hit"; journal wf_13c0f539)
findings.title: Settings popover: focus does not move into it or back, and it sits after the panel in the DOM
where: skills/talk/static/call.js:213-221 (showPop only toggles hidden and aria-expanded, with no focus move and no return of focus on Escape)
skills/talk/static/call.html:70 (#pGear is role=dialog placed after the aside, outside #panel)
skills/talk/static/call.js:221 (Escape only closes the pop)
findings.evidence: Settings reported 'expanded' but its contents were not found in the tree Daniel read. Escape gave no sign that it had closed. Tabbing past Talk led nowhere.
findings.cause: The popover is declared as a dialog without any focus management. It is not next to its button in reading order, so the screen-reader cursor does not reach it after pressing the button. Closing it leaves focus on whatever had it.
findings.reproduced: code reading. The screenshot shows the popover has real, labelled content (including the autoplay toggle), so the defect is reachability and focus.

skeptics.correction: Mostly accurate. Two things to adjust. (1) The claim that the popover contents "were not found in the tree" is not shown by the code. The DOM node exists once it is unhidden, so it is reachable only by the screen reader's browse cursor or by Tab at the end of the document, not by the button's own position. (2) The same applies to #pCalls, which is probably also outside the panel, and to the rail gear (#railgear), which uses the same pop. Severity "minor" is fair, or slightly higher for keyboard and screen-reader users because they cannot reach the settings easily.

Severity "minor" is fair. The finding is code-based, and the persona's "its contents were not found in the tree" could be a tool limitation. The same applies to the calls popover (pCalls), which uses the same showPop. The line cited as 213-221 is right. Line 257 also closes the popover when the stage takes focus. aria-controls is already set on the buttons, but that does not move focus or reading order.

Two details are overstated. First, focus is not lost on close: the button that opened the popover keeps focus, because nothing moves it, so the real defect is that focus never enters the dialog and Escape gives no announcement. Second, the claim that the popover's contents were "not found in the tree" is probably an effect of DOM order and the missing focus move, not a hidden-content bug. The popover is reachable by Tab, but only after the whole aside. Also, aria-controls is set on the buttons. Minor severity is fair.

findings.guard_proof: focus-rail: without fix (popChanged empty): "AssertionError: assert ['', ['pKeys'...], [None, '']] == ['railgear', ...None, 'gear']] 1 failed in 0.23s"; with fix: '1 passed in 0.22s'
findings.note: Same hook as S-keyboard-1: focus moves into the dialog on open, Tab is kept inside, focus returns to the opener on close (rail gear and the Keys sheet opened from the gear included). The dialog still sits after the panel in the DOM, which no longer matters since focus is moved into it.

findings.source: study finding screenreader-7 (details.html, "What the testers hit"; journal wf_13c0f539)
findings.title: The current sentence is shown twice, in the reader overlay and in the conversation, and the reader has no role
where: skills/talk/static/call.html:19 (#reader is a div with aria-label but no role; the label is ignored on a generic div)
skills/talk/static/call.js:913-962 (paintReader rebuilds the answer text word by word in spans)
skills/talk/static/call.html:22 (the panel is the aside 'The call')
findings.evidence: Daniel heard the current sentence twice. One copy is loose text outside the 'The call' landmark, the other is in the answer entry.
findings.cause: The reader is a visual copy of the answer on the stage side, placed outside the panel landmark. It is neither aria-hidden nor a labelled region, so it is read as loose duplicated text.
findings.reproduced: code reading

skeptics.correction: Minor corrections. (1) The reader is hidden (display:none, mode "off") when idle or at rest with a board in front, so the duplication only exists while an answer plays, or at rest in "text" mode. (2) In text mode the reader holds the whole answer, but sentences not yet said are `visibility:hidden`, so a screen reader meets only the current and past sentences. In strip mode only the current sentence is displayed. Say "the answer text so far", not only "the current sentence". (3) The cited line range 913-962 is right for the reader code. Severity minor is reasonable.

Severity is minor, and "hear" is the right need. The reader is only displayed while it has text (.reader.text is display:block, otherwise display:none), so the duplicate appears only while an answer is being read or shown. The label on a role-less div is not announced in most readers, which is correct. The fix is either aria-hidden on #reader, since the conversation holds the same text, or a role="region" with the label. Cite call.js paintReader by function name rather than by the line range 913-962, which I did not check.

Two small corrections. First, the page is only a pure duplicate while the reader is shown, meaning while it has the `text` class or the `strip` layout, not at all times. Second, the fault is not mainly that the label is ignored on a generic div. It is that a visual copy of the answer is exposed to assistive tech. The fix is likely `aria-hidden="true"` on `#reader`, so only the panel's entry is read, plus the live-region handling the panel already has.

findings.guard_proof: WITHOUT (aria-label back, aria-hidden gone): 1 failed in 0.08s | WITH: 1 passed in 0.06s
findings.notice: A screen reader no longer reads the playing sentence twice.
findings.note: #reader is a picture of the answer the panel holds, so it is aria-hidden and has no label.

findings.source: study finding interrupter-1 (details.html, "What the testers hit"; journal wf_13c0f539)
findings.title: A correction does not stop the superseded answer: it arrives after the correction and plays aloud over the new board
where: skills/talk/static/call.js:833-835 (maybeAutoplay stale guard looks only at you-entries listed AFTER the answer)
skills/talk/static/call.js:1443 (sendText pauses only what already plays)
skills/talk/talk.py:2203 (while_working: the correction is folded into the same turn, so the late answer to turn 1 is entered after it)
findings.evidence: Sofia sent a plan, then 'no wait, only 10 days, Kyoto first' while Claude worked. Answer 1 (the 14-day plan) then arrived and played its rail-pass sentence while the stage already showed the 10-day board. Answer 2 sat queued. Voice and screen disagreed.
findings.cause: Staleness is decided by list position only. The correction was sent while turn 1 was being answered, so the answer to turn 1 lands after the 'you' entry in the list. The guard sees nothing newer after it and autoplays it. It does not know the answer is for a turn that a later message has already amended. The stage also shows its board. Nothing marks the answer outdated. The next answer then waits in the queue behind it.
findings.reproduced: code reading plus shot 05: answer 1 sits below the 'no wait' message and plays with a pause button; answer 2 is queued

skeptics.correction: Describe the cause as follows. The order of entries decides staleness, and an answer entered after a while_working correction counts as fresh. Whether the late answer already reflects the correction depends on when the responder collected the turn. The stage showing the 10-day board while the 14-day answer is spoken is real in the code, and it is not a harness artifact. Severity "major" is arguable, because the user can pause the answer and the next one is queued behind it. The "Next answer ready" and "1 days" notes in the diary are separate issues.

Minor. The stage showed board 2 of 2 at that moment, so the mismatch is between the voice, the caption and the stage board, not wrong text on the stage. The exact lines are approximate: the guard is at call.js ~832-835 and the sendText pause is at ~1443. The same gap exists in `startQueued`. Severity "major" is plausible but arguable: answer 2 does arrive and plays after answer 1, and a later case in the diary (messages 4 and 5) was handled correctly, because there the stale answer was entered before the newer "you" entry.

The cause is overstated as purely the page's. The reply to turn 1 is stale mainly because the responder answered turn 1 without folding in the correction. `offer` marks the correction `while_working` and sends it as an addition to the same turn, which a real session would read together. The page cannot tell whether a reply already covers a `while_working` message that precedes it. So the page-side defect is narrower. It plays a reply that follows a `while_working` addition, without checking that the reply covers it. A cheap guard would not autoplay a reply while a later turn is still open (a reply to turn 1 followed by a pending reply to the correction), or would play the newest one. Severity: moderate rather than major. It needs a slow responder and a correction sent mid-work, and the page's own skip logic handled the other cases.

findings.guard_proof: Server test, FIX REMOVED (the `or call.added_to_since(turn_id)` term taken out): KeyError: 'superseded' at test_wait_server.py:387 / 1 failed in 0.34s. FIX RESTORED: 1 passed in 0.29s. Pins the late reply superseded True with kind 'addition', speech 'skipped', and only 'Ten days, Kyoto first.' spoken. The page test is a regression pin that also passes without the fix. Output: .scratch/run/evidence/W1/interrupter-removed.txt and interrupter-restored.txt
findings.notice: When you send a correction while Claude is still answering, the earlier answer is tagged as replaced and never read aloud, even if Claude had already picked your correction up as its own question. Only the answer to the correction plays.
findings.note: Reopened case: a correction sent while Claude worked (plain Send, while_working, no replaces) was collected as t2 before t1 was answered, so the late answer 1 was shown untagged and spoken. New Call.added_to_since(turn_id) is true when a non-withdrawn, non-cancelled while_working entry belongs to a later turn than the one being answered; post_reply tags that reply superseded (kind addition, never spoken, no board). The true replaces case was already tagged correction and is now pinned. The page already refuses to autoplay or queue a superseded entry.
findings.reopen_note: Round 1 (re-check reproduces on r1-re-t6; shot 05-later.png). The build covers a correction that is still uncollected when the old turn is answered. When the responder has already collected the correction as its own turn (t2) before it replies to t1, the late answer 1 is shown, gets no Replaced tag and is read aloud; the server answers plain 'sent'. FIX: server side, when a reply for a turn arrives and a later 'you' entry carries `replaces` naming that turn's entry (the correction, talk.py about 2221-2228), tag the reply superseded even if the correction was collected as its own turn (check in the code that replace() gives the correction that field in this case); page side, such an answer is never autoplayed or queued, as for the other superseded case. GUARD: server test with correction collected as t2 then reply to t1 -> superseded; page test unchanged for no autoplay.

findings.source: study finding interrupter-2 (details.html, "What the testers hit"; journal wf_13c0f539)
findings.title: A queued answer announces 'Next answer ready' with no way to skip it, and a replaced answer is not marked outdated
where: skills/talk/static/call.js:519 (queued status text, no action)
skills/talk/static/call.js:817-826 (startQueued drops it silently only if a newer you-entry is after it)
findings.evidence: While answer 1 played, the foot read 'Next answer ready: it plays when this one ends.' Sofia could not tell whether it was still worth hearing. The foot has no Skip or Cancel. Answers she had replaced look the same as current ones in the list; only 'Play' differs.
findings.cause: The queued state is a plain text line in the status area, not a control. The only quiet drop is the same position-based check as in interrupter-1, so a stale queued answer is announced anyway. No per-answer 'superseded' state exists in the entries or the conversation.
findings.reproduced: code reading plus shot 05

skeptics.correction: Minor. A user can get around the queue by pressing Play on another answer, or by pausing, because the queued answer starts only on the audio "ended" event. The queue line itself still has no control. The "replaced answers look the same" part is also narrower than stated. `maybeAutoplay` (around lines 835-841) already refuses to autoplay or queue an answer when a newer "you" entry follows it, so staleness is only possible when the user speaks after the answer was queued. The `startQueued` check then drops it silently, and no "outdated" mark is shown. Severity minor is right.

The cause is partly misdescribed. The queued answer in shot 05 (answer 2) is the fresh one, so announcing it is correct. The stale item is the answer playing (answer 1). maybeAutoplay (about lines 835-836) already refuses to queue an answer when a later you-entry exists, so a stale queued answer is not announced. The real gap is narrower. The correction does not stop the playing outdated answer, superseded answers carry no mark, and the foot has no Skip or Play-next control. Jumping is possible through the Play link on the queued answer's row. Line 519 is right. Cite about 819-823 and 835-836 for the drop logic. Minor severity is fair.

Three corrections. (1) The cause is not the same as in interrupter-1. The drop check does exist and does handle the case where the user spoke after the queued answer. What is missing is any user control over the queue, so the cause is "no control and no staleness state", not "position-based check fails". (2) The page does give a way to act. Playing or tapping the queued answer's entry loads it and clears the queue (call.js:769). Pausing leaves the queue in place, since startQueued runs only on the audio "ended" event (call.js:827). Treat the cause as unsettled. The finding's guess (`wordFloors` measuring before the font or Greek glyphs were ready) is plausible, because `wordFloors` runs once from `shapeBoard`, and the ResizeObserver reruns it only when the wrap's width changes by more than 1 px. Do not rule out the `--w` shares as the cause: column 1 is a `td.key`, and `.md.grid td.key` sets `width:auto`. The "blocker" severity looks overstated. The overlap is confined to the stage's table board, the panel and call flow still work, the answer text carries the same content, and the persona saw only one table and one headless Chromium. "Major, stage-only" fits better. The finding is also not necessarily Greek-specific, since any font that loads late could trigger it, and the claim that "no `board:` line warned the responder" is true but expected, because the server cannot know about client-side layout. findings.title: Table board columns collide: Who is drawn over When
where: skills/stage/static/stage.js:549-551 (css .md.grid col width max(var(--w),var(--min)) with table-layout fixed, stage.css:549-550)

findings.cause: With table-layout fixed, each column's width is max(percentage share, --min). The shares are computed from text length, and wordFloors measures floors from a canvas. The columns that hold the long words come out narrower than the bold text, and the cells have no overflow clipping, so the text spills into the next column. The 4-row table is not stepped, so no row is lit to widen it. I did not reproduce which of the two inputs fails.

skeptics.correction: Mark the cause as unconfirmed. The early return in wordFloors when wrap.clientWidth is 0 is not enough to explain a collision that persists, because the ResizeObserver re-measures once the width becomes nonzero. The more likely suspects are a stale or incorrect --min, for example from the font fallback at measure time or from the key column's td.key rule (width:auto), or the colgroup percentages overriding the floors. The scope (stage-only) and the major severity are fair. The text is unreadable in the persona's view, though it may depend on the font load timing and viewport.

The cause is unverified: the analyst did not reproduce it, and I did not either. The cited lines are roughly right. The col width rule is stage.css:550 and the table-layout rule is stage.css:549. The percentage shares are at stage.js ~578-588 and wordFloors is at ~607-636. The code reads the failure as "the percentage shares are too small", but those shares are only a fallback. The mechanism that should prevent a collision is --min, so the real question is why --min came out too small or never got set. The candidates are canvas measurement before the font loaded, an early return at clientWidth 0 with no later re-run, or a font-family string that the canvas resolves differently. The "4-row table is not stepped" remark is irrelevant to the cause. Severity "major" is fair for a table whose cells cannot be read, but the claim that normal users would meet it is plausible rather than proven.

Keep the finding, but state the cause as unconfirmed. I did not reproduce it either. The cause is probably not the percentage shares from text length. The `--min` floor is meant to override them, and it evidently did not apply here. More likely `--min` was never set or was too small. Either `wordFloors` ran with `clientWidth` 0, or the canvas measured with a fallback font before the page font loaded. The ResizeObserver only reruns it when the width changes, so it never reruns after the font loads. That could be partly specific to headless Chromium. Also, the quoted lines 549-551 are in stage.css, not stage.js. "Major" is fair for the stage but arguably should be "moderate", because the table is still partly readable and the finding is stage-only. No finding in the side panel is affected.

skeptics.correction: Two corrections. First, the fold is a CSS line-clamp of 1, not a "first sentence" cut, so the visible text is the first line of the answer at the panel width. Second, the cited line ranges (320-329 and 388-414) are slightly off: the fold is built at about lines 322-329 and the stick-to-end logic is in render() at about lines 388-414. Severity "major" is arguable, since the browser's own find-in-page does not reach folded text beyond the clamp.

"No topic label" is overstated. Each answer sits directly under the user's own question, shown in full in the "You" bubble, and often under board chips such as "Turn path", "How a turn waits" and "Stalled rule" (see shot 02-02). Those work as a topic for a call the user typed. They help less for spoken turns, whose question text may be vague, and they do not help when the answer to a question lives in the middle of a later answer. The missing piece is search across answer text, plus the cut-off first sentence being a weak summary. Folded text is still in the DOM (a line-clamp, not display:none), so browser find may match it but would not unfold it. The "opens scrolled to the end" part is by design, since render sticks to the end when the reader was at the end. Severity "major" looks high. "Minor to moderate" fits better, because Show text is one tap and the question above each answer gives context.

Severity "major" is overstated. Treat it as moderate or minor. The user's own turns are not folded (the fold applies only to `e.who === "claude"`), so each answer sits under the full question that prompted it. That question works as a topic label, and the persona's report of "no topic" misses it. Opening the list scrolled to the end is ordinary chat behaviour, not a defect. The accurate claim is that the panel has no search and that the folded line is only the answer's first sentence, which may not name its subject. Cause: by design the panel does not show answer text, so lookup depends on the question lines and on Show text.

findings.title: Audio and waits table: columns overlap (EVENT/AUDIO FILES, Restart/stay, reused)
where: skills/stage/static/stage.js:607-638 wordFloors measures each column's longest word on a canvas and sets --min
skills/stage/static/stage.css:549-550 table-layout:fixed and col{width:max(var(--w),var(--min))}
skills/stage/static/stage.css:545 wrapper width min(100%,var(--tw)) in ch
findings.evidence: A narrow 3-column table board has headers and cells colliding in the first column. 'Restart' runs into 'stay, reused', and 'EVENT' into 'AUDIO FILES'. The first column's words wrap to two lines and crowd the next column. The table is small and floats in a large empty area.
findings.cause: Probable: the column floor is measured once with canvas text metrics (weight forced to at least 600, only the first measure and later wrap-width changes re-run it). If the webfont is not loaded at that time, or the bold weight differs from the measured one, the floor is a few pixels too small. The fixed layout then lets the text overflow into the next cell. Not confirmed by a re-run.
findings.reproduced: not reproduced; code reading of wordFloors against the overlap in the shot

skeptics.correction: Mark the cause as unconfirmed. A canvas measuring bold text before the webfont loads, or a font mismatch, is only one candidate. The first column holds `td.key` cells at weight 600, and the floor is measured at max(600, weight), so that part should be right. Other candidates are a floor that is not applied or that is overridden by `--w`, and a ResizeObserver that never re-runs the measure after the fonts load. The line references are slightly off: the `table-layout:fixed` and `col` rules are at about stage.css 548-549, and the wrapper width rule is at about 545. Scope is stage-only. Severity "major" is arguable, because the table is small and legible apart from the two collisions, but the overlap itself is real.

The suggested cause, a floor "a few pixels too small", does not fit the shot. The column is short by the full cell padding (36 px) plus about 2 px, and that is the amount `wordFloors` adds on top of the measured word width. That points to `--min` being unset or computed against a stale or zero width, not to a webfont metric difference. Likely candidates are `wordFloors` returning early when `wrap.clientWidth` is 0 at first paint, or the ResizeObserver skipping a re-measure. The cause is still unconfirmed. The cited lines are right, but the cause should be marked as a guess, and the claim that the table "floats in a large empty area" is cosmetic and not part of the bug. The "major" rating is arguable, since the text is still legible, but the collisions are real.

The proposed cause (a floor "a few pixels too small" from a webfont or bold-weight mismatch) does not fit the shots. Column 1 is only about 41 px wide, measured from the cell edge at x=301 and the column 2 text at x=360 less its 18 px padding. "Restart" in bold needs roughly 55 px plus 36 px of padding. A weight or font mismatch would miss by a pixel or two, not by half. In the code, wordFloors (stage.js:607-638) always puts at least the column's padding plus 2 px into --min. So the floor looks as if it was never applied to column 1, rather than slightly small. Candidates to check: wordFloors returning early on `!avail || !wordSum` and the ResizeObserver not re-running it; or `col{width:max(var(--w),var(--min,0px))}` (stage.css:550) not being honoured on a `<col>` under table-layout:fixed, so the percentage --w wins. Column 1 gets a tiny --w share because its short text, "Call ends", sets the narrow width. The cited css line 545 is the wrapper width rule, not the cause. The finding should be kept as a stage-only table-layout bug, severity major or somewhat lower, with the cause marked unconfirmed.

findings.title: Table board: row labels print on top of the next column
where: skills/stage/static/stage.js:607-636 wordFloors sets each col's --min from measured words
skills/stage/static/stage.css:210 .tablewrap .key{width:1%;white-space:nowrap}
skills/stage/static/stage.css:550 .md.grid col{width:max(var(--w),var(--min))}
findings.evidence: On the table board the first column's text (Concurrency, Backups, Migrations, Hosting, Monthly cost) is drawn over the SQLite cells ('none extra', 'one writer', 'copy a file'). The header row also has three titles (SQLITE, POSTGRES, MANAGED) over four visible columns, so the headers sit one column out. It stayed broken on the 6-row redo (the settings shot shows it again, even in the 6-row table).
findings.cause: Not reproduced in code alone. Likely the first (row-label) column has an empty header and a narrow width (the 1% key rule), while its cell text is wider than the floor wordFloors computed. The floor is measured in the cell's computed font (weight at least 600, but the th/key font may differ), and the nowrap key cell then spills over the neighbour. The row-label column has no header, so the three header cells are misaligned with the four data columns. Cause not confirmed by running it.
findings.reproduced: code reading only; seen in two screenshots

skeptics.correction:
Two parts of the finding are wrong.

1. The header is not misaligned. The table has four columns: an empty first header over the row labels, then SQLITE, POSTGRES and MANAGED. In the shots those three titles sit over their own columns (x about 242, 460 and 679). `shapeBoard` (stage.js 556-575) gives every column its own `th`, `td` and `col`. The real defect is only the label column being too narrow, so the labels spill into the next cell.

2. The cause given is wrong. The rule at stage.css 210 (`.tablewrap .key{width:1%;white-space:nowrap}`) is overridden on board tables by `.md.grid td.key{width:auto;white-space:normal}` (line 553). The cell text should wrap, not spill because of nowrap. The likelier cause is that `--min` was never set, or was set too small, for the key column. `wordFloors` returns early when `wrap.clientWidth` or the word sum is 0, which happens if the board is measured while hidden or before fonts load, and the ResizeObserver only re-measures on a width change. Treat this as unconfirmed.

Severity "blocker" is probably high. The text is readable but ugly, and every row label overlaps its neighbour.

The header claim is overstated. The three titles (SQLITE, POSTGRES, MANAGED) sit over the three data columns, so they are not "one column out". The first column has an empty header, which is expected. The real defect is that the key (row-label) column is far too narrow for its text. Two things in the code point to the cause. In stage.css, line 210 sets `.tablewrap .key{width:1%;white-space:nowrap}` and line 553 sets `.md.grid td.key{width:auto;white-space:normal}`. And `.md.grid table` uses `table-layout:fixed`, with `col` width `max(var(--w),var(--min))`. In that fixed layout the key column's `--min` or `--w` evidently does not cover the label width, so the text overflows into the next column. Why `wordFloors` (stage.js 607-636) underestimates the floor for that column is not established. Possible reasons are the font used to measure, the `data-c` indexing, or padding. Treat the cause as unconfirmed. Also, "blocker" is arguably too high. It is stage-only, and the table is still readable, though ugly. Call it high or major.

Three parts of the finding are wrong.

1. The header misalignment claim is false. SQLITE, POSTGRES and MANAGED line up with the data columns that start at about x=242, x=460 and x=679. The header row has an empty first cell over the label column, so there are four header cells for four data columns.

2. The cited cause is wrong. `shapeBoard` (stage.js ~546-600) sets `--w` per column from the text, and `wordFloors` sets `--min` from measured words. Both are applied in `.md.grid col{width:max(var(--w),var(--min))}` on a fixed-layout table (stage.css:550). The `.tablewrap .key{width:1%;white-space:nowrap}` rule at stage.css:210 is overridden for `.md.grid` by `td.key{width:auto;white-space:normal}` at stage.css:553. So the cited line 210 does not explain it, and the rendered width does not match what the code should produce.

3. The cause is unconfirmed. Some rule makes the key column about 60 px wide and not its computed `max(--w, --min)`. The place to look is where `--w` and `--min` are applied for the empty-header key column. The finding should be reworded as: "the key column of a board table with an empty first header renders too narrow, and its words overflow into the next column".

Severity is overstated as a blocker. It affects only the stage table board and makes the first column hard to read; the table is not lost. Major is more accurate.

The cut is not a dead end. `.code` has `overflow:auto` and `.lines` is `width:max-content` (stage.css lines 123-125), so the board scrolls sideways and the cut text can be reached. A phone wraps by default. The real gap is that nothing signals the clipped line, such as a fade or scrollbar, and the board shows no overflow cue in the screenshot. Two points are overstated. (1) The cut is not data loss. `.code` is `overflow:auto`, so the box scrolls sideways and the full line can be reached. The user does not have to use Wrap lines. Two corrections. (1) The cause is only partly the page. The activity items come from the session's activity hook posting to /api/activity (talk.py `record_activity`). The responder agents in this harness may fire that hook late or rarely, so a real /talk session may show a label and seconds much sooner. I did not verify this against the hook. The page-owned part is that the fallback, when no activity has arrived, shows no elapsed time or label. (2) The cited lines are slightly off. The fallback text is at call.js:527 in the `view.working` branch. Lines 331-332 are about the fold button and do not render status entries, so that citation is wrong.
